doc.title: Tom Scott interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 1, 2022 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Current projects: radio show, TikTok, teaching and producing Brittni Paiva
summary: Scott discusses his radio show, TikToks, upcoming album and a Grammy-winning Hawaiian production.

story.theme_name: Still working: current gigs, upcoming projects and plans
story.community_name: What's next: upcoming tours, records and plans

blocks.x: What’s on your docket these days?

Well right now of course I’m doing some gratis work. Of course I’ve got my podcast, I’ve got a radio show on KJZZ which is the Southern California jazz station, I’ve got a weekly jazz show there called “Hang Time with Tom Scott.” I’m doing of course I’ve done a lot of — I got on Tik Tok at the recommendation of the guy who is now my producer in Connecticut actually, and so I’ve got a whole series of Tik Toks where they’re sort of two part Tik Toks. The first one is where I play that portion of a record where I’ve soloed. And I’ll take that, I bought a green screen and so I will mime that solo in this green screen and then send that to my guy in Connecticut and he puts the album, the cover of the album I’m playing, if it’s Carole King “Jazzman” or Paul McCartney and Wings, whatever it is, in the background. That’s one Tik Tok and then the second one is where I talk, “Yes I did play the solo on Carole King’s ‘Jazzman’ and here’s how it happened.” And I tell the story of going to the studio and like that. So I must have probably thirty pairs of Tik Toks. I’m @TomScottJazzman if anybody wants to look. And so there’s that, the radio show, I’m also — well I’ve got, I’m still working on my upcoming, I’m doing an album here, probably this summer. And it’s going to be, I hate to say L.A. Express, because it could end up being the New York Express. We’re still debating whether to do it — I’m going to New York in July to teach as I have done two or three years back at the Summer Jazz Program. This year oddly enough I’ll be teaching audio engineering which of course I have done but I’ve done it from the standpoint of a musician. There’s actually three of us: me, and then there’s a guy who actually is a fulltime audio engineer. He is the engineer for “Saturday Night Live” among other things. But he’s I think on staff at NYU where this is taking place. And the third guy is like a hip hop guy, a loop guy. So between the three of us they’ll get a real full picture of what it’s like sitting at a board, and of course I am proud to say that I am a Hawaiian Grammy winning producer. I produced a record for a young girl named Brittni Paiva who © Fillius Jazz Archive -24-

is a wonderful ukulele player in Hawaii and we did a whole album with her, some jazz tunes, some folky, folkish kind of tunes, even one classical tune. We did the Faure “Pavane” kind of in the style of a Bill Evans with a symphony orchestra record. And except for her playing and a couple of jazz soloists that I got on the record, Arturo Sandoval, Ray Parker and Michael McDonald did a whole bunch of vocals on one of his tunes. But the rest was all me: drums and bass and keyboards and strings and everything, and engineered it. And for that, so I do know how a board works. And of course back in the days when I was doing my own records regularly my engineer Hank Cicalo, well there were other engineers but primarily he’s the one that comes to mind because I did L.A. Express, New York Connection, all that stuff with him. He would, on a 24-track machine he’s got 24 faders there. So he would take the front 16, which was the drums, the rhythm section basically, and I would take the back 8 which would be all the overdubs, the saxes, woodwinds, anything else. So we would mix the thing, manually of course in those days, there was no automatic floating faders, well there were but we didn’t have them. And so we did it all manually. And so I do know the board, and so I can bring some wisdom to that area I hope.
